claim: Under hypoxic conditions, some organisms use an electron transport chain consisting of only complex I and II (CII) to generate the proton gradient essential for ATP production.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, some organisms use an electron transport chain consisting of only complex I and II (CII) to generate the proton gradient essential for ATP production.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with established knowledge about anaerobic metabolism.

claim: In hypoxic conditions, CII functions as a fumarate reductase that accepts electrons from a low electron potential quinol, rhodoquinol (RQ).
source: In these cases, CII functions as a fumarate reductase that accepts electrons from a low electron potential quinol, rhodoquinol (RQ).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about anaerobic electron transport chains.

claim: RquA is very patchily distributed across eukaryotes and bacteria adapted to hypoxia.
source: RquA is very patchily distributed across eukaryotes and bacteria adapted to hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic distribution data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses suggest lateral gene transfer (LGT) of rquA from bacteria to eukaryotes occurred at least twice.
source: Phylogenetic analyses suggest lateral gene transfer (LGT) of rquA from bacteria to eukaryotes occurred at least twice and the gene was transferred multiple times amongst protists.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses and topology tests presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rquA gene was transferred multiple times amongst protists.
source: Phylogenetic analyses suggest lateral gene transfer (LGT) of rquA from bacteria to eukaryotes occurred at least twice and the gene was transferred multiple times amongst protists.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses showing non-monophyletic relationships among protist sequences.

claim: RquA functions in the mitochondrion-related organelles of the anaerobic protist Pygsuia.
source: We demonstrate that RquA functions in the mitochondrion-related organelles of the anaerobic protist Pygsuia and is correlated with the presence of RQ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing colocalization with MitoTracker.

claim: The presence of RquA in Pygsuia is correlated with the presence of RQ.
source: We demonstrate that RquA functions in the mitochondrion-related organelles of the anaerobic protist Pygsuia and is correlated with the presence of RQ.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing RQ species in Pygsuia.

claim: In aerobic eukaryotes, complexes I (CI) and II (CII) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain oxidize reduced cofactors generated by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (NADH and FADH2 respectively) and reduce the lipid-soluble electron carrier ubiquinone (UQ) to ubiquinol (UQH2).
source: In aerobic eukaryotes, complexes I (CI) and II (CII) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) oxidize reduced cofactors generated by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (NADH and FADH2 respectively) and reduce the lipid-soluble electron carrier ubiquinone (UQ) to ubiquinol (UQH2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial electron transport.

claim: Complex III (CIII) oxidizes UQH2 and transfers electrons to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV, CIV; via cytochrome c) and eventually to O2, converting it to H2O.
source: Complex III (CIII) oxidizes UQH2 and transfers electrons to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV, CIV; via cytochrome c) and eventually to O2, converting it to H2O (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aerobic respiration and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: CI, CIII, and CIV generate a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane that fuels oxidative phosphorylation of ADP to ATP by the F1-Fo ATP synthase (Complex V, CV).
source: In the process, CI, CIII, and CIV generate a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane that fuels oxidative phosphorylation of ADP to ATP by the F1-Fo ATP synthase (Complex V, CV).
evidence: This is established knowledge about oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: The ETCs of facultative anaerobes have adapted to function in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors.
source: However, the ETCs of facultative anaerobes have adapted to function in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors (Kita et al., 1988; Tielens, 1994; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the adult stage of Ascaris suum, CIII and CIV are down-regulated but CI continues to oxidize NADH and pump protons.
source: For example, in the adult stage of Ascaris suum, CIII and CIV are down-regulated but CI continues to oxidize NADH and pump protons (Sakai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakai et al., 2012.

claim: In Ascaris suum, CI transfers electrons from NADH to the quinone, rhodoquinone (RQ), generating rhodoquinol (RQH2).
source: In this organism, CI transfers electrons from NADH to the quinone, rhodoquinone (RQ), generating rhodoquinol (RQH2).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Ascaris metabolism.

claim: RQH2 is reoxidized by CII functioning as a fumarate reductase (FRD), reducing fumarate to succinate.
source: RQH2 is reoxidized by CII functioning as a fumarate reductase (FRD), reducing fumarate to succinate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about anaerobic metabolism.

claim: The adult Ascaris mitochondrial ETC is able to generate a proton gradient to fuel ATP synthesis, even in the absence of oxygen.
source: Thus, the adult Ascaris mitochondrial ETC is still able to generate a proton gradient to fuel ATP synthesis, even in the absence of oxygen (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: RQ is structurally similar to UQ but possesses an amino group instead of a methoxy group on the quinone ring.
source: RQ is structurally similar to UQ but possesses an amino group instead of a methoxy group on the quinone ring (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the chemical structures in Figure 1B.

claim: The lower electron potential of RQ (−63 mV), compared to UQ (+100 mV), favors the FRD reaction.
source: The lower electron potential of RQ (−63 mV), compared to UQ (+100 mV), favors the FRD reaction (Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005.

claim: RQ has been detected in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: RQ has also been detected in other eukaryotes that experience hypoxia including Caenorhabditis elegans (Takamiya et al., 1999), parasitic helminths (Kita et al., 1988; Van Hellemond et al., 1996), Euglena gracilis (Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and Nyctotherus ovalis (Boxma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takamiya et al., 1999.

claim: RQ has been detected in parasitic helminths.
source: RQ has also been detected in other eukaryotes that experience hypoxia including Caenorhabditis elegans (Takamiya et al., 1999), parasitic helminths (Kita et al., 1988; Van Hellemond et al., 1996), Euglena gracilis (Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and Nyctotherus ovalis (Boxma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kita et al., 1988 and Van Hellemond et al., 1996.

claim: RQ has been detected in Euglena gracilis.
source: RQ has also been detected in other eukaryotes that experience hypoxia including Caenorhabditis elegans (Takamiya et al., 1999), parasitic helminths (Kita et al., 1988; Van Hellemond et al., 1996), Euglena gracilis (Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and Nyctotherus ovalis (Boxma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005.

claim: RQ has been detected in Nyctotherus ovalis.
source: RQ has also been detected in other eukaryotes that experience hypoxia including Caenorhabditis elegans (Takamiya et al., 1999), parasitic helminths (Kita et al., 1988; Van Hellemond et al., 1996), Euglena gracilis (Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and Nyctotherus ovalis (Boxma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boxma et al., 2005.

claim: The presence of RQ in mitochondria or related organelles of other anaerobic eukaryotes has not been established.
source: However, the presence of RQ in mitochondria or related organelles of other anaerobic eukaryotes has not been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: Mitochondrion-related organelles (MROs) are specialized mitochondria found in anaerobic protistan lineages that have evolved to function in low oxygen conditions.
source: Mitochondrion-related organelles (MROs) are specialized mitochondria found in anaerobic protistan lineages that have evolved to function in low oxygen conditions (Stairs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stairs et al., 2015.

claim: The properties of MROs vary between organisms ranging from the simple 'mitosomes' of Giardia intestinalis to the 'hydrogenomes' of Trichomonas vaginalis.
source: The properties of MROs vary between organisms ranging from the simple 'mitosomes' of Giardia intestinalis, that appear to function solely in iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster generation, to the 'hydrogenomes' of Trichomonas vaginalis, or 'hydrogen-producing mitochondria' of Nyctotherus ovalis that couple ATP generation to hydrogen production (for review see Stairs et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Mitosomes of Giardia intestinalis appear to function solely in iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster generation.
source: The properties of MROs vary between organisms ranging from the simple 'mitosomes' of Giardia intestinalis, that appear to function solely in iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster generation, to the 'hydrogenomes' of Trichomonas vaginalis, or 'hydrogen-producing mitochondria' of Nyctotherus ovalis that couple ATP generation to hydrogen production (for review see Stairs et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Hydrogenomes of Trichomonas vaginalis couple ATP generation to hydrogen production.
source: The properties of MROs vary between organisms ranging from the simple 'mitosomes' of Giardia intestinalis, that appear to function solely in iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster generation, to the 'hydrogenomes' of Trichomonas vaginalis, or 'hydrogen-producing mitochondria' of Nyctotherus ovalis that couple ATP generation to hydrogen production (for review see Stairs et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Hydrogen-producing mitochondria of Nyctotherus ovalis couple ATP generation to hydrogen production.
source: The properties of MROs vary between organisms ranging from the simple 'mitosomes' of Giardia intestinalis, that appear to function solely in iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster generation, to the 'hydrogenomes' of Trichomonas vaginalis, or 'hydrogen-producing mitochondria' of Nyctotherus ovalis that couple ATP generation to hydrogen production (for review see Stairs et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The reduction or remodeling of the respiratory chain is of central importance to the ATP-generating function of MROs.
source: Of the various adaptations to anaerobiosis, the reduction or remodeling of the respiratory chain is of central importance to the ATP-generating function of the resulting organelles.
evidence: This is based on inference from the role of the respiratory chain in ATP generation.

claim: Some anaerobic protists have completely lost all components of the respiratory chain.
source: Some anaerobic protists have completely lost all components of the respiratory chain, while others have maintained all or parts it (Stairs et al., 2015;Gawryluk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stairs et al., 2015 and Gawryluk et al., 2016.

claim: Some anaerobic protists have maintained all or parts of the respiratory chain.
source: Some anaerobic protists have completely lost all components of the respiratory chain, while others have maintained all or parts it (Stairs et al., 2015;Gawryluk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stairs et al., 2015 and Gawryluk et al., 2016.

claim: RQ has been proposed to function as an electron carrier in the respiratory chains of some anaerobic protists.
source: While RQ has been proposed to function as an electron carrier in the respiratory chains of some of these protists (Müller et al., 2012; Gawryluk et al., 2016), the presence of RQ has not been described.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Müller et al., 2012 and Gawryluk et al., 2016.

claim: Biochemical and genetic investigations of Rhodospirillum rubrum have demonstrated that UQ is a precursor to RQ.
source: Recently, biochemical and genetic investigations of the alphaproteobacterium Rhodospirillum rubrum have demonstrated that UQ is a precursor to RQ (Brajcich et al., 2010), and that a putative methyltransferase (since named RquA) is essential for RQ biosynthesis and anaerobic growth (Lonjers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brajcich et al., 2010.

claim: A putative methyltransferase (RquA) is essential for RQ biosynthesis and anaerobic growth in Rhodospirillum rubrum.
source: Recently, biochemical and genetic investigations of the alphaproteobacterium Rhodospirillum rubrum have demonstrated that UQ is a precursor to RQ (Brajcich et al., 2010), and that a putative methyltransferase (since named RquA) is essential for RQ biosynthesis and anaerobic growth (Lonjers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lonjers et al., 2012.

claim: A total of 182 RquA sequences were retrieved from unique taxonomic units.
source: We retrieved a total of 182 sequences from unique taxonomic units (i.e., NCBI taxonomy ID) and reduced this dataset to 166 sequences based on a sequence identity cutoff of less than 90%.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection process.

claim: The dataset was reduced to 166 sequences based on a sequence identity cutoff of less than 90%.
source: We retrieved a total of 182 sequences from unique taxonomic units (i.e., NCBI taxonomy ID) and reduced this dataset to 166 sequences based on a sequence identity cutoff of less than 90%.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: The rquA gene is extremely rare in bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: The rquA gene is extremely rare in bacteria and eukaryotes, and we could not identify homologs in any publicly available archaeal genomes.
evidence: This is based on the results of database searches.

claim: RquA homologs could not be identified in any publicly available archaeal genomes.
source: The rquA gene is extremely rare in bacteria and eukaryotes, and we could not identify homologs in any publicly available archaeal genomes.
evidence: This is based on the results of database searches.

claim: RquA genes are found among sparse representatives of only seven different orders of alpha-, beta- and gammaproteobacteria.
source: RquA genes are found among sparse representatives of only seven different orders of alpha-, beta- and gammaproteobacteria (Burkholderiales, Magnetococcales, Neisseriales, Rhizobiales, Rhodobacteriales, Rhodocyclales and Rhodospirillales).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic distribution analysis.

claim: Within eukaryotes, rquA homologs were identified in 24 representatives of four of the five super-groups of eukaryotes (Obazoa, Amoebozoa, Sar, and Excavata).
source: Within eukaryotes, we identified rquA homologs in 24 representatives of four of the five super-groups of eukaryotes (Obazoa, Amoebozoa, Sar, and Excavata; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on database searches and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The rquA gene could not be found in the vast majority of eukaryotic genomes and transcriptome surveys available on Genbank.
source: The gene could not be found in the vast majority of eukaryotic genomes and transcriptome surveys available on Genbank (summarized in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: rquA was identified in Pygsuia biforma, but not in its close relatives, Breviata anathema and Lenisia limosa.
source: Within breviates, we identified rquA in Pygsuia biforma, but not in its close relatives, Breviata anathema and Lenisia limosa, despite the ample genomic and transcriptomic data available for the latter (Hamann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on database searches and is supported by a citation to Hamann et al., 2016.

claim: Spliceosomal introns were identified in the rquA genes in eukaryotic taxa for which genomic records were available.
source: We identified spliceosomal introns in the rquA genes in eukaryotic taxa for which genomic records were available (i.e., Proteromonas lacertae, Mastigamoeba balamuthi, Brevimastigomonas motovehiculus, Reticulomyxa filosa, and all the Blastocystis subtype genomes) indicating that these are in fact eukaryotic sequences and not prokaryotic contaminants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of spliceosomal introns in eukaryotic rquA genes indicates that these are eukaryotic sequences and not prokaryotic contaminants.
source: We identified spliceosomal introns in the rquA genes in eukaryotic taxa for which genomic records were available (i.e., Proteromonas lacertae, Mastigamoeba balamuthi, Brevimastigomonas motovehiculus, Reticulomyxa filosa, and all the Blastocystis subtype genomes) indicating that these are in fact eukaryotic sequences and not prokaryotic contaminants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the inference that spliceosomal introns are characteristic of eukaryotic genes.

claim: The Proteromonas and Blastocystis rquA gene sequences showed conservation of intron position and size.
source: The Proteromonas and Blastocystis rquA gene sequences showed conservation of intron position and size.
evidence: This is based on genomic sequence analysis.

claim: None of the other eukaryotic rquA gene sequences (for which genomic sequence was available) shared intron positions.
source: But none of the other eukaryotic rquA gene sequences (for which genomic sequence was available) shared intron positions.
evidence: This is based on genomic sequence analysis.

claim: A potential contaminating sequence was identified in the mollusk Aplysia (Bioproject:PRJNA77701, Accession number:GBCZ01101516).
source: We did identify a potential contaminating sequence in the mollusk Aplysia (Bioproject:PRJNA77701, Accession number:GBCZ01101516).
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: The Aplysia rquA homolog was 89% identical to the Neoparamoeba amino acid sequence.
source: This homolog was 89% identical to the Neoparamoeba amino acid sequence and could derive from a Neoparamoeba-related parasite present in the Aplysia tissue.
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: The Aplysia rquA homolog could derive from a Neoparamoeba-related parasite present in the Aplysia tissue.
source: This homolog was 89% identical to the Neoparamoeba amino acid sequence and could derive from a Neoparamoeba-related parasite present in the Aplysia tissue.
evidence: This is based on inference from sequence similarity and the presence of Neoparamoeba-like sequences in the same project.

claim: Small subunit sequence (GBCZ01078303.1) that is 93% identical to Neoparamoeba aestuarina was identified in the Aplysia sequencing project.
source: Indeed, we were able to identify small subunit sequence (GBCZ01078303.1) that is 93% identical to Neoparamoeba aestuarina in this sequencing project.
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: Despite the presence of RQ in some animals (e.g., A. suum and C. elegans), homologues of rquA could not be detected in these genomes.
source: Despite the presence of RQ in some animals (e.g., A. suum and C. elegans) we were unable to detect homologues of rquA in these genomes.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic RquA homologs formed a maximally supported clade that emerged from within a group of bacterial ubiquinone/menaquinone biosynthesis C-methyltransferase proteins.
source: Preliminary phylogenetic analyses showed that prokaryotic and eukaryotic RquA homologs formed a maximally supported clade that emerged from within a group of bacterial ubiquinone/menaquinone biosynthesis C-methyltransferase proteins (Supplementary file 2, tree 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The deepest split in the RquA clade is between two distinct groups of homologs (Group A and B) composed of prokaryotic and eukaryotic sequences of mixed taxonomic affinities.
source: The deepest split in the RquA clade as shown is between two distinct groups of homologs (here referred to as Group A and B) composed of prokaryotic and eukaryotic sequences of mixed taxonomic affinities (Figure 2, Supplementary file 2, tree 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The split between Group A and Group B receives maximal support in both ML and Bayesian analyses in the unrooted RquA tree.
source: This split receives maximal support in both ML and Bayesian analyses in the unrooted RquA tree (Figure 2, Supplementary file 2, tree 2), as well as the larger analysis (Supplementary file 2, tree 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Group A comprises sequences from alphaproteobacteria, betaproteobacteria and metagenome samples, as well as five distinct eukaryote lineages.
source: The Group A clade comprises sequences from alphaproteobacteria, betaproteobacteria and metagenome samples, as well as five distinct eukaryote lineages (the breviate Pygsuia, the stramenopiles Blastocystis and Proteromonas, three amoebozoans Mastigamoeba, Copromyxa and a Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba group, euglenids and the rhizarian Brevimastigamonas).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Group B contains alpha-, beta- and gammaproteobacterial homologs, candidate phylum radiation (CPR) bacterial sequences and four independent lineages of eukaryotes.
source: Group B contains alpha-, beta- and gammaproteobacterial homologs, candidate phylum radiation (CPR) bacterial sequences and four independent lineages of eukaryotes (the opisthokont Monosiga ovata, a ciliate clade, a diatom group and a rhizarian amoebae group).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In Group A, Blastocystis + Proteromonas grouped strongly with the parasitic amoebozoan Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba clade and the euglenids.
source: In Group A, Blastocystis + Proteromonas (gut stramenopile protists) grouped strongly with the parasitic amoebozoan Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba clade and the euglenids, despite the fact that none of these lineages are closely related in the tree of eukaryotes (i.e. they branch from within the three fundamental eukaryotic 'mega-groups' of Diaphoretickes, Amorphea and Excavata respectively).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Blastocystis, Proteromonas, Neoparamoeba, Paramoeba, and euglenids are not closely related in the tree of eukaryotes.
source: In Group A, Blastocystis + Proteromonas (gut stramenopile protists) grouped strongly with the parasitic amoebozoan Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba clade and the euglenids, despite the fact that none of these lineages are closely related in the tree of eukaryotes (i.e. they branch from within the three fundamental eukaryotic 'mega-groups' of Diaphoretickes, Amorphea and Excavata respectively).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of eukaryotic phylogeny.

claim: A weakly supported sister group to the Blastocystis + Proteromonas + Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba + euglenids clade was formed by a clade of homologs from six metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) from a human gut metagenome study.
source: A weakly supported sister group to this eukaryotic subtree was formed by a clade of homologs from six metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) from a human gut metagenome study (Nielsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2014.

claim: The MAG sequences appear to be a subgroup of the Rhodospirillales alphaproteobacteria.
source: These appear to be a subgroup of the Rhodospirillales alphaproteobacteria (see below and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), that we henceforth refer to as 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All other eukaryotes in Group A branch in distinct positions in the A-subtree, with very poor support in the backbone of the tree.
source: All other eukaryotes in Group A branch in distinct positions in the A-subtree, with very poor support in the backbone of the tree.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The breviate Pygsuia, the rhizarian Brevimastigamonas and the amoebozoans Mastigamoeba and Copromyxa were weakly excluded from the Blastocystis + Proteromonas + Neoparamoeba + Paramoeba + euglenids + MAG Azo/Aceto grouping.
source: The breviate Pygsuia, the rhizarian Brevimastigamonas and the amoebozoans Mastigamoeba and Copromyxa were also weakly excluded from the above eukaryote + 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria grouping; each of these instead branched independently amongst bacterial groups in Group A.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Group B was poorly resolved.
source: Group B was similarly poorly resolved, although a number of branches separating the eukaryote groups from each other did receive ultrafast bootstrap support of >90% (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: A topology in which Group A and B eukaryotes were constrained to form a single clade in the tree to the exclusion of the bacterial sequences was strongly rejected (p-value = 3×10−37).
source: A topology in which Group A and B eukaryotes were constrained to form a single clade in the tree to the exclusion of the bacterial sequences was strongly rejected (p-value = 3×10−37, Table 1, Supplementary file 2, tree 2).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: All topologies constraining the monophyly of major eukaryotic lineages, except monophyletic amoebozoans, were rejected with p-values < 0.05.
source: All topologies, except monophyletic amoebozoans (found only in Group A) were rejected with p-values < 0.05 (Table 1, Supplementary file 2 trees 2–15).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: Monophyletic eukaryotes in Group A could not be rejected (p-value = 0.253).
source: Tests of relationships within Group A or within Group B separately revealed that monophyletic eukaryotes in each subtree could not be rejected if each were constrained one at a time (p-value = 0.253 for Group A eukaryote monophyly and p-value = 0.179 for Group B eukaryote monophyly).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: Monophyletic eukaryotes in Group B could not be rejected (p-value = 0.179).
source: Tests of relationships within Group A or within Group B separately revealed that monophyletic eukaryotes in each subtree could not be rejected if each were constrained one at a time (p-value = 0.253 for Group A eukaryote monophyly and p-value = 0.179 for Group B eukaryote monophyly).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: The monophyly of alphaproteobacteria was firmly rejected (p-value = 5×10−34).
source: We first tested the monophyly of alphaproteobacteria as a whole (Supplementary file 2, tree 18) and found this was firmly rejected (p-value = 5×10−34), confirming our observation that alphaproteobacteria were phylogenetically interspersed throughout the RquA tree.
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: Alphaproteobacteria are phylogenetically interspersed throughout the RquA tree.
source: We first tested the monophyly of alphaproteobacteria as a whole (Supplementary file 2, tree 18) and found this was firmly rejected (p-value = 5×10−34), confirming our observation that alphaproteobacteria were phylogenetically interspersed throughout the RquA tree.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and topology tests.

claim: The monophyly of eukaryotes + all alphaproteobacteria was rejected with p-value < 0.01.
source: We then tested: (i) the monophyly of eukaryotes + all alphaproteobacteria, (ii) the monophyly of all Group A eukaryotes + all Group A alphaproteobacteria, and the monophyly of all Group B eukaryotes + all Group B alphaproteobacteria. All of these topologies were rejected with p-values < 0.01 (Supplementary file 2, trees 18–21).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: The monophyly of all Group A eukaryotes + all Group A alphaproteobacteria was rejected with p-value < 0.01.
source: We then tested: (i) the monophyly of eukaryotes + all alphaproteobacteria, (ii) the monophyly of all Group A eukaryotes + all Group A alphaproteobacteria, and the monophyly of all Group B eukaryotes + all Group B alphaproteobacteria. All of these topologies were rejected with p-values < 0.01 (Supplementary file 2, trees 18–21).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: The monophyly of all Group B eukaryotes + all Group B alphaproteobacteria was rejected with p-value < 0.01.
source: We then tested: (i) the monophyly of eukaryotes + all alphaproteobacteria, (ii) the monophyly of all Group A eukaryotes + all Group A alphaproteobacteria, and the monophyly of all Group B eukaryotes + all Group B alphaproteobacteria. All of these topologies were rejected with p-values < 0.01 (Supplementary file 2, trees 18–21).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: A topology containing a clade of all Group A eukaryotes + 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria was not rejected (p-value = 0.227).
source: However, a topology containing a clade of all Group A eukaryotes + 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria was not rejected (p-value = 0.227; Supplementary file 2, tree 17).
evidence: This is based on approximately unbiased (AU) topology tests.

claim: rquA-encoding alphaproteobacterial genomes are patchily distributed, emerging as numerous isolated groups within several orders of the alphaproteobacteria.
source: A maximum likelihood phylogeny estimated from this matrix shows that rquA-encoding alphaproteobacterial genomes are patchily distributed, emerging as numerous isolated groups within several orders of the alphaproteobacteria (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Group A- and Group B-containing taxa are interspersed in the alphaproteobacterial phylogeny.
source: Group A- and Group B-containing taxa are interspersed.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: Genomes encoding rquA are extremely rare within the alphaproteobacterial orders.
source: Genomes encoding the gene are extremely rare within the alphaproteobacterial orders.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenomic analysis and genome survey.

claim: Five alphaproteobacterial orders (Rickettsiales, Holosporales, Pelagibacterales, Sphingomonadales, and Caulobacterales) had no rquA-containing taxa out of a total of 455 genomes examined.
source: Five alphaproteobacterial orders (Rickettsiales, Holosporales, Pelagibacterales, Sphingomonadales, and Caulobacterales) had no rquA-containing taxa (out of a total of 455 genomes examined).
evidence: This is based on genome survey data.

claim: The Rhizobiales order had rquA-containing taxa in 7 out of 514 genomes examined.
source: The remaining three orders had rquA-containing taxa in 7 out of 514 (Rhizobiales), 6 out of 513 (Rhodobacterales) and 21 out of 217 (Rhodospirillales).
evidence: This is based on genome survey data.

claim: The Rhodobacterales order had rquA-containing taxa in 6 out of 513 genomes examined.

claim: Most aerobic model system eukaryotes possess the majority of Q-utilizing systems in their mitochondria.

source: However, for the eukaryote sequences of the A-type, the affinities of the 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria to some of the eukaryotic sequences could implicate this gut-dwelling lineage of the Rhodospirillales as donors.

claim: The 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial genomes encode other enzymes of anaerobic metabolism including [FeFe]-Hydrogenase and its maturase enzymes HydE-G.
source: This is particularly intriguing since the same genomes encode other enzymes of anaerobic metabolism including [FeFe]-Hydrogenase and its maturase enzymes HydE-G (Degli Esposti et al., 2016; Leger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degli Esposti et al., 2016 and Leger et al., 2016.

claim: Several 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial homologs of hydrogenase metabolism show affinities to some (but not all) eukaryotic homologs.
source: Although several of these 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial homologs of hydrogenase metabolism show affinities to some (but not all) eukaryotic homologs, others appear to be more distantly related to eukaryotes (and to each other) suggesting multiple independent origins by LGT (see supplementary figures S3-S6 from Leger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leger et al., 2016.

claim: The 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria acquired the hydrogen and rhodoquinone metabolism genes from other anaerobic bacteria relatively recently in a series of LGT events.
source: We propose that the 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria acquired the hydrogen and rhodoquinone metabolism genes from other anaerobic bacteria relatively recently in a series of LGT events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the phylogenetic data.

claim: After the initial lateral transfer of A- and B-type genes into recipient eukaryotes, the rquA sequences must have acquired mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS).
source: In any case, after the initial lateral transfer of A- and B-type genes into recipient eukaryotes, the rquA sequences must then have acquired mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS).
evidence: This is based on inference from the presence of MTS in eukaryotic sequences.

claim: The subsequent transfers of MTS-containing rquA genes between different eukaryotes could have allowed them to adapt their mitochondrial ETCs to low-oxygen conditions.
source: The subsequent transfers of MTS-containing rquA genes between different eukaryotes could then have allowed them to adapt their mitochondrial ETCs to low-oxygen conditions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference.

claim: Additional data from more eukaryotic and prokaryotic taxa harbouring rquA should improve the resolution of the phylogeny.
source: Additional data from more eukaryotic and prokaryotic taxa harbouring rquA (perhaps from metagenomic investigations of low-oxygen environments) should improve the resolution of the phylogeny and will allow the relative merits of the various evolutionary origin scenarios to be re-assessed in future.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research.

claim: The role and enzymatic activity of RquA in RQ biosynthesis is currently unclear.
source: The role and enzymatic activity of RquA in this reaction is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Lonjers et al. (2012) outline three hypotheses for the role of RquA in RQ biosynthesis.
source: Lonjers et al. (2012) outline three hypotheses for the role of RquA in RQ biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lonjers et al., 2012.

claim: The first hypothesis is that RquA could serve a regulatory role in the expression of currently unknown RQ biosynthesis proteins.
source: The first hypothesis is that RquA could serve a regulatory role in the expression of currently unknown RQ biosynthesis proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claim: It is unlikely that RquA has a role in regulating the expression of nuclear genes in the nucleus.
source: Since the vast majority of mitochondrial proteins (and all of those involved in quinone biosynthesis) are encoded by nuclear genes and we have shown that RquA functions in mitochondria, it is unlikely that RquA has a role in regulating the expression of such genes in the nucleus (although it could participate in post-transcriptional, or post-translational regulation).
evidence: This is based on inference from the mitochondrial localization of RquA and the nuclear location of most mitochondrial genes.

claim: A second hypothesis is that UQ and RQ are synthesized by different multi-enzyme complexes in R. rubrum that share some components.
source: A second hypothesis is that UQ and RQ are synthesized by different multi-enzyme complexes in R. rubrum that share some components.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claim: Some components of the yeast UQ biosynthesis complex are necessary for stabilization of the complex independent of their catalytic role.
source: This is based on the observation that some components of the yeast UQ biosynthesis complex are necessary for stabilization of the complex independent of their catalytic role (Baba et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baba et al., 2004.

claim: If RquA served to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex, one would expect all organisms that encoded RquA would also have to encode UQ biosynthesis proteins.
source: If this were the case for RQ biosynthesis, one would expect all organisms that encoded RquA would also have to encode UQ biosynthesis proteins.
evidence: This is based on logical inference.

claim: Many of the eukaryotes that encode RquA do not encode any components of the UQ biosynthesis pathway.
source: However, many of the eukaryotes that encode RquA do not encode any components of the UQ biosynthesis pathway (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys.

claim: It is very improbable that RquA serves to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex.
source: It is therefore very improbable that RquA serves to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex.
evidence: This is based on inference from the absence of UQ biosynthesis genes in some RquA-containing organisms.

claim: The final hypothesis is that RquA is directly involved in catalyzing the conversion of UQ to RQ.
source: The final hypothesis is that RquA is directly involved in catalyzing the conversion of UQ to RQ.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claim: RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5.
source: Since RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5 (Supplementary file 2, tree 1), RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
source: Since RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5 (Supplementary file 2, tree 1), RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
evidence: This is based on inference from the relationship to UbiE/Coq5.

claim: No enzyme is known that catalyzes a one-step amino-transfer reaction with a methoxy leaving group.
source: Although it is tempting to suggest that RquA directly converts UQ to RQ in one step, no enzyme is known that catalyzes a one-step amino-transfer reaction with a methoxy leaving group.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of enzyme mechanisms.

claim: It seems more plausible that either RquA alone catalyzes a multi-step reaction sequence, or is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway involving at least a demethylation step followed by an amino-transfer reaction.
source: It seems more plausible that either: (i) RquA alone catalyzes a multi-step reaction sequence, or, (ii) is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway involving at least a demethylation step followed by an amino-transfer reaction.
evidence: This is based on speculation about the enzymatic mechanism.

claim: No other enzyme with the same restricted phylogenetic distribution as rquA was found amongst bacterial or eukaryotic homologs using phylogenetic profiling.
source: We were unable to find any other enzyme with the same restricted phylogenetic distribution as rquA amongst bacterial or eukaryotic homologs using phylogenetic profiling (i.e., assessing co-presence of genes within rquA-containing but not rquA-lacking organisms).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic profiling analysis.

claim: If RquA is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway, another broadly-conserved enzyme with a different main biochemical function in bacteria and in mitochondria could, as a moonlighting side-reaction, catalyze a step of RQ biosynthesis.
source: Therefore, it seems likely that, if option (ii) were correct, another broadly-conserved enzyme with a different main biochemical function in bacteria and in mitochondria could, as a moonlighting side-reaction, catalyze a step of RQ biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on speculation about the enzymatic mechanism.

claim: Under either scenario, the lateral transfer of the rquA gene could, in principle, confer on the recipient the ability to convert UQ to RQ.
source: Under either of these scenarios, then, the lateral transfer of the rquA gene could, in principle, confer on the recipient the ability to convert UQ to RQ.
evidence: This is based on speculation about the consequences of LGT.

claim: Further experimental work will be needed to test the hypotheses about RquA function.
source: Clearly, further experimental work will be needed to test these hypotheses.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The acquisition of rquA by LGT was a key early step in the evolutionary transitions to anaerobic mitochondrion-related organelles.
source: The acquisition of rquA by LGT as described herein, was a key early step in these transitions; the selective benefit of this acquisition seems relatively clear.
evidence: This is based on inference from the evolutionary scenario.

claim: The ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups likely resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes.
source: For example, assuming that the ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes (Figure 5, 'aerobic mitochondria'), it is likely that they would occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of whether they are in marine, freshwater, or terrestrial environments.
evidence: This is a speculative assumption based on comparison to modern organisms.

claim: Aerobic protistan groups would likely occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of their environment.
source: For example, assuming that the ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes (Figure 5, 'aerobic mitochondria'), it is likely that they would occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of whether they are in marine, freshwater, or terrestrial environments.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of environmental conditions.

claim: During transient exposure to anoxia, CIII and CIV fail to function efficiently and are downregulated.
source: During transient exposure to anoxia, it is known from model systems that CIII and CIV fail to function efficiently and are downregulated (Vijayasarathy et al., 2003; Fukuda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vijayasarathy et al., 2003 and Fukuda et al., 2007.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions, shifts in mitochondrial metabolism occur: reduced UQ (UQH2) builds up, the NADH/NAD + ratios increase, and part of the TCA cycle reverses.
source: Furthermore, under hypoxic conditions (e.g., in ischemia-reperfusion injury or solid tumours), shifts in mitochondrial metabolism occur: reduced UQ (UQH2) builds up because of the lack of CIII/CIV activity, the NADH/NAD + ratios increase as CI throughput is repressed, and part of the TCA cycle reverses (Tomitsuka et al., 2010; Chouchani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomitsuka et al., 2010 and Chouchani et al., 2014.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions, malate is imported from the cytosol (or produced in mitochondria) and is converted to fumarate by fumarase.
source: Under these conditions, malate is imported from the cytosol (or produced in mitochondria) and is converted to fumarate by fumarase.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of mitochondrial metabolism under hypoxia.

claim: At sufficiently high UQH2 and fumarate concentrations, CII will function in fumarate reduction to regenerate UQ and succinate.
source: At sufficiently high UQH2 and fumarate concentrations, CII will function in fumarate reduction to regenerate UQ (Ackrell et al., 1993) and succinate.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ackrell et al., 1993.

claim: The 'NADH:fumarate reductase system' allows CI to continue to function to pump protons and oxidize NADH.
source: This 'NADH:fumarate reductase system' allows CI to continue to function to pump protons and oxidize NADH (Tomitsuka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tomitsuka et al., 2010.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions, CI and CII produce high levels of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Under these conditions, however, it is known that CI and CII produce high levels of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) Tomitsuka et al., 2010; Chouchani et al., 2014.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomitsuka et al., 2010 and Chouchani et al., 2014.

claim: If an organism frequently encountering low-oxygen conditions were to acquire rquA by LGT and express the gene, the organism would be able to synthesize and utilize low electron potential RQ as an electron carrier.
source: Thus, if an organism frequently encountering these low-oxygen conditions were to acquire rquA by LGT and express the gene, the organism would able to synthesize and utilize low electron potential RQ as an electron carrier.
evidence: This is based on inference from the function of RQ.

claim: RQ would greatly enhance the efficiency of the LGT recipient's NADH:fumarate reductase system leading to an increase in proton pumping of CI, restoration of ATP synthesis and decreased ROS production.
source: RQ would greatly enhance the efficiency of the LGT recipient's NADH:fumarate reductase system leading to an increase in proton pumping of CI, restoration of ATP synthesis and decreased ROS production.
evidence: This is based on inference from the properties of RQ and the function of the NADH:fumarate reductase system.

claim: The foregoing scenario is likely why rquA was retained after acquisition by protists with canonical mitochondria that can function aerobically and anaerobically such as Euglena and a number of ciliates.
source: The foregoing scenario is likely why rquA was retained after acquisition by protists with canonical mitochondria that can function aerobically and anaerobically such as Euglena (Hoffmeister et al., 2004; Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and a number of the ciliates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on inference from the evolutionary scenario and is supported by citations.

claim: The acquisition of rquA is likely one of the first steps in the evolution of anaerobic MROs found in protists such as Brevimastigamonas, Blastocystis, Mastigamoeba, and Pygsuia.
source: We propose that the acquisition of rquA is likely one of the first steps in the evolution of anaerobic MROs found in protists such as Brevimastigamonas, Blastocystis, Mastigamoeba, and Pygsuia.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the evolutionary scenario.

claim: In lineages adapted to hypoxic environments, there has been further reductive evolution in their ETC.
source: In these lineages, there has been further reductive evolution in their ETC, as they have adapted to thrive predominantly in hypoxic environments.
evidence: This is based on inference from the reduced ETC components in these organisms.

claim: CIII and CIV of the electron transport chain of Brevimastigamonas motovehiculus appears to be degenerating with components missing or becoming pseudogenes.
source: For example, CIII and CIV of the electron transport chain of the recently described rhizarian anaerobe Brevimastigamonas motovehiculus appears to be degenerating with components missing or becoming pseudogenes (Gawryluk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gawryluk et al., 2016.

claim: Blastocystis spp. completely lack CIII-CV.
source: The parasites Blastocystis spp. have gone further in this reduction; they completely lack CIII-CV (Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; Gentekaki et al., 2017) and therefore none of their ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; and Gentekaki et al., 2017.

claim: None of the ATP in Blastocystis spp. is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The parasites Blastocystis spp. have gone further in this reduction; they completely lack CIII-CV (Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; Gentekaki et al., 2017) and therefore none of their ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the absence of CIII-CV.

claim: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi.
source: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi (Figure 5), as both completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
source: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi (Figure 5), as both completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of CI, it is unclear how Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi can be reducing the oxidized RQ produced by CII.
source: In the absence of CI, it is unclear how these two organisms can be reducing the oxidized RQ produced by CII.
evidence: This is based on inference from the absence of CI.

claim: Most quinone-binding proteins in Pygsuia and Mastigamoeba typically catalyze redox reactions with reduction potentials far greater than RQ reduction and thus would be expected to oxidize RQH2 rather than reduce RQ.
source: Most of their quinone-binding proteins typically catalyze redox reactions with reduction potentials far greater than RQ reduction and thus would be expected to oxidize RQH2 rather than do the opposite.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of redox potentials.

claim: One possibility is that the electron transferring flavoprotein (ETF)/ETF-dehydrogenase (ETF-DH) systems of Pygsuia and Mastigamoeba are able to gain electrons by oxidizing reduced NADH.
source: One possibility is that the electron transferring flavoprotein (ETF)/ETF-dehydrogenase (ETF-DH) systems of these organisms (which usually function in fatty acid oxidation) are able to gain electrons by oxidizing reduced NADH.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: ETF/ETF-DH could oxidize NADH by electron bifurcation with butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase, as is known to occur in some bacteria.
source: This could occur by electron bifurcation with butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase, as is known to occur in some bacteria (Chowdhury et al., 2014; Chowdhury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowdhury et al., 2014 and Chowdhury et al., 2015.

claim: Bacterial ETF alpha and beta subunits can coordinate two FAD cofactors (instead of one as in mitochondrial ETF), allowing for electron bifurcation.
source: These bacterial ETF alpha and beta subunits can coordinate two FAD cofactors (instead of one as in mitochondrial ETF), allowing for electron bifurcation (Roberts et al., 1996; Chowdhury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 1996 and Chowdhury et al., 2015.

claim: An alternative possibility in Pygsuia is that NADH oxidation could be achieved by two remaining conserved subunits of CI, NuoE and NuoF, working together with ETF/ETF-DH system.
source: An alternative possibility in Pygsuia is that NADH oxidation could be achieved by two remaining conserved subunits of CI, NuoE and NuoF (Stairs et al., 2015), working together with ETF/ETF-DH system.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to Stairs et al., 2015.

claim: NuoE and F are thought to be involved in oxidation of NADH and ferredoxin in conjunction with [FeFe]-hydrogenase in many anaerobic protists to produce molecular hydrogen.
source: NuoE and F are thought to be involved in oxidation of NADH and ferredoxin in conjunction with [FeFe]-hydrogenase in many anaerobic protists to produce molecular hydrogen (Stairs et al., 2015; Hamann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stairs et al., 2015 and Hamann et al., 2016.

claim: If ETF could oxidize a low redox potential cofactor (e.g., NADH and/or ferredoxin), it could pass the electrons on ETF-DH that could replenish the RQH2 pool in Pygsuia and Mastigamoeba.
source: In any case, if ETF could oxidize a low redox potential cofactor (e.g., NADH and/or ferredoxin), it could pass the electrons on ETF-DH (present in both Pygsuia and Mastigameoba) that could replenish the RQH2 pool in these organisms (shown by arrows in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Biochemical studies of the ETCs in anaerobic protists will be critical to test the hypotheses about electron transfer.
source: Biochemical studies of the ETCs in these anaerobic protists will be critical to test these hypotheses.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The gene encoding RquA was likely transferred from bacteria to various eukaryote lineages by multiple independent events of LGT, well after the establishment of mitochondria within eukaryotes.
source: The gene encoding RquA, an enzyme required to synthesize RQ, was likely transferred from bacteria to various eukaryote lineages by multiple independent events of LGT, well after the establishment of mitochondria within eukaryotes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: RquA was subsequently transferred between some eukaryotes via LGT.
source: RquA was then subsequently transferred between some eukaryotes via LGT, although the directions of these transfers cannot be easily discerned.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The directions of eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfers of rquA cannot be easily discerned.
source: RquA was then subsequently transferred between some eukaryotes via LGT, although the directions of these transfers cannot be easily discerned.
evidence: This is based on the poor resolution of the phylogeny.

claim: LGTs of rquA likely conferred the ability to biosynthesize RQ in mitochondria, making it possible for complex II to efficiently reduce fumarate to succinate, allowing the recipient eukaryotes to respire in the absence of oxygen.
source: Regardless, these LGTs likely conferred the ability to biosynthesize RQ in mitochondria, making it possible for complex II to efficiently reduce fumarate to succinate, allowing the recipient eukaryotes to respire in the absence of oxygen.
evidence: This is based on inference from the function of RQ and the experimental data.

claim: This is a stark example of how laterally acquired enzymes can interface with ancestral pathways in mitochondria to rapidly adapt these organelles to low oxygen conditions.
source: This is a stark example of how laterally acquired enzymes can interface with ancestral pathways in mitochondria to rapidly adapt these organelles to low oxygen conditions (Stairs et al., 2014; Nývltová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings and is supported by citations to Stairs et al., 2014 and Nývltová et al., 2015.
